Almost every country that eats chocolate is grey on this map. Cocoa grows in a band roughly 20 degrees either side of the equator and effectively nowhere else.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The near-black spot on the West African coast is Côte d'Ivoire: the largest producer on Earth by a wide margin, around 45% of world output in 2024. Add Ghana next door and the two clear 60% between them.

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)
2/ It hasn't always sat there. Ghana led the world until 1978, when Côte d'Ivoire overtook it. Indonesia had almost no cocoa industry in the 1970s and was the world's second producer by 2006.

3/ The plant isn't African. Theobroma cacao comes from the upper Amazon, was carried north into Mesoamerica long before Europeans arrived, and only reached West Africa in the colonial era. Its biggest producer is a transplant.

4/ The grey is the actual story. Producing countries aren't consuming countries: roughly 70% of global chocolate sales happen in the rich world. The bean crosses the equator; most of the money never crosses back.
5/ 2024 showed what that costs. Cocoa had traded near $2,500 a tonne since the 1980s. On 13 June 2024 it hit $11,530 in London. The year before, it had averaged $3,182.

6/ The causes sit in the dark patches: bad weather, black pod, and cacao swollen shoot virus. Ghana's cocoa board reported 81% of the crop in its main growing region hit by the virus, and delayed 350,000 tonnes of deliveries.

7/ The part that surprises people: record prices didn't make growers rich. Ivorian and Ghanaian beans are sold forward at fixed government prices before the season. The spike happened in a futures market farmers aren't in.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
